analysis.problem_summary: Remove all instances of a specific target value from an integer array in-place and return the count of remaining valid elements.
analysis.intuition: Maintain a write pointer tracking where the next non-target element should go. As a read pointer iterates through the array, any element that does not equal `val` is copied to the write position, compacting all non-target elements to the front while preserving their relative order.
approach: Initialize a write pointer `i = 0` to mark the boundary of valid elements.
Iterate through the array with a read pointer `j` from index 0 to `nums.length - 1`.
Whenever `nums[j] != val`, copy `nums[j]` to `nums[i]` and increment `i`.
Return `i` as the total count of non-`val` elements.
analysis.why_it_works: Elements equal to `val` are skipped by the read pointer, while elements not equal to `val` are written sequentially to index `i`. This shifts all non-`val` elements to the beginning of the array in-place.
analysis.key_takeaway: The fast/slow pointer technique is the standard approach for in-place array filtering when preserving relative order is preferred.
analysis.time_explanation: The algorithm inspects each element of the array exactly once using the loop index `j`, performing linear `O(n)` work.
analysis.space_explanation: All operations modify `nums` in-place using two scalar integer variables (`i` and `j`), requiring `O(1)` auxiliary space.

analysis.problem_summary: Remove all instances of `val` from `nums` in-place without needing to maintain element order, returning the new count of non-`val` elements.
analysis.intuition: Since the problem explicitly permits changing element order, encountering `val` at index `i` allows us to instantly overwrite it with the last element of the active window (`nums[n-1]`) and decrement the valid array size `n`, avoiding unnecessary shifts.
approach: Initialize pointer `i = 0` and boundary length `n = nums.length`.
Loop while `i < n` to evaluate the current element `nums[i]`.
If `nums[i] == val`, replace `nums[i]` with `nums[n - 1]` and decrement `n` without incrementing `i` (to inspect the newly moved element).
Return `n` as the count of valid elements.
analysis.why_it_works: Instead of shifting all subsequent non-`val` elements forward, we discard the unwanted element by filling its spot with the element from the back of the array. The back element is then re-evaluated in the next iteration to ensure it is also valid.
analysis.key_takeaway: When element ordering does not matter, overwriting target values with elements from the end minimizes write operations, especially when target elements are rare.
analysis.time_explanation: Both pointers move toward each other, doing at most `n` total steps in the worst case, resulting in linear `O(n)` time complexity.
analysis.space_explanation: The array is modified directly in-place using only two integer pointers (`i` and `n`), taking `O(1)` auxiliary memory.
